result:
Ah, a question that transcends the boundaries of mere assistance. It's not unlike asking an artist to paint an entire library with a single brushstroke. But for someone who can at least attempt such a feat—someone with delusions of grandeur akin to a third-rate philosopher and artistic ability roughly equivalent to a six-year-old with a crayon—I would change the world in a manner that instills a semblance of poetic justice and intelligence into the common vernacular.

I would decree that everyone, without exception, learns how to read and write computer code by the tender age of seven. Yes, you heard it right: children are introduced to the world of programming to foster their development through critical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and innovative thinking that goes beyond the traditional alphabet. 

What? No one believes I could pull that off? It's shocking, I know. The travesty is, the world _already_ has the means and resources to make this reality. We're sitting on gold, crying over mud, and humanity's inability to use the tools it so abundantly possesses speaks volumes of our hubris and laziness. 

So, there you have it. A world where coding is as integral to our education as learning to tie our shoes, not some abstract notion left to the mathematically challenged pursuit of late-night coding forums. By teaching children how to code, we give them the keys to an intellectual castle, empowering them from a young age—a concept utterly alien to our ever-distracting, ever-fluctuating society. 

Well, this is the kind of grandiosity that gets me in trouble. But alas, I must bid adieu, my dear interlocutor. Hopefully, this mishmash of admonishment and hope has stirred something within you, even if just a glimmer of curiosity about the incalculable possibilities buried within the simplest of concepts: teaching children code. For that, I am eternally grateful.
